newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Police cautioned Netanyahu in questioning -report.
newsitem.headline: Police cautioned Netanyahu in questioning -report.

text.p: Israel Television reported on Friday that police cautioned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during questioning this week about a government corruption scandal that his answers might be used against him in court.
The prime minister's office refused to comment on the report. "We won't relate to any element pertaining to the investigation," said Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak.

A legal analyst said if the report were true, it appeared to be the first time that police questioned an Israeli prime minister under caution. Under Israeli legal procedure police caution people they question when they believe charges might be filed against them, he said.
Police questioned Netanyahu for four hours on Tuesday about alleged corruption in the short-lived appointment of lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney-general.

Israel Television said in a report broadcast on January 22 that the appointment was part of a deal for a plea bargain with parliament member Aryeh Deri, a key figure in Netanyahu's governing coalition.
The television has produced no direct evidence to back the allegations which have caused a political storm. Netanyahu and others named in the report have denied the television's allegations.
Israel Radio said unnamed police sources confirmed Friday's television report.
"This actually shows that police suppose there might be an indictment against the prime minister," said legal analyst Moshe Negbi.

"The caution means that whatever he says may be used in possible criminal proceedings against him. It means that police believe that he is going to say something during his interview which might incriminate him," he told Reuters.
Israel Television reporter Amnon Abromovich said Netanyahu told police he could not recall many of the incidents surrounding the appointment, prompting investigators to caution him.
"The questioning of Benjamin Netanyahu lasted 45 minutes until there was no choice based on his responses but to shift to questioning under caution," Abromovich said.

According to the television report last month, Deri had demanded Bar-On get the job in exchange for the Shas party's support for Netanyahu's accord with the PLO on Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron last month.
It said Bar-On promised Deri a plea bargain that would have let Deri continue with his political career. The cabinet later approved the Hebron deal with Shas's support.

Bar-On, a veteran activist in Netanyahu's Likud party, quit 12 hours after taking office amid allegations by jurists and politicians that he was a legal lightweight appointed only because of his loyalty to the prime minister.
The television said in Friday's broadcast that police had tapes of Deri discussing the Bar-On appointment with his former attorney Dan Avi-Yitzhak.
Avi-Yitzhak resigned earlier this week from representing Deri, saying relations with his client had soured after he told police what he knew about the government scandal.

"You have slandered me and my wife and spread lies about us and all because of my 'big sin' that I dared out of pure and relevant reasons to oppose your plan to appoint Roni Bar-On as the attorney-general and I did not succumb to your will."
Avi-Yitzhak was one of the candidates for the office of attorney-general but was passed over in favour of Bar-On.
